analysis.one_liner: Cancels existing medical debt and bars interest, aggressive collection, and credit reporting of medical bills.
analysis.headline: A bill to cancel Americans' medical debt was introduced in May 2024 with 13 House sponsors, sent to two committees, and never received a hearing or a vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would direct the Health and Human Services Department to run a grant program paying hospitals to wipe out every eligible medical debt their patients owe, then expand the program to other providers and individuals. Going forward, it would require hospitals and other providers to screen patients for charity care before billing, send bills in plain language, stop charging interest on past-due medical bills, and cap what nonprofit hospitals can charge uninsured patients. It would also make it illegal under federal debt-collection law to collect any medical debt that existed when the law passed, and would erase medical debt from credit reports.
analysis.who_benefits: Tens of millions of Americans carrying medical debt: their existing hospital bills would be canceled by federal grants, debt collectors would be barred from pursuing pre-existing medical debt, medical debt would disappear from credit reports within 30 days, and future bills could no longer accrue interest.

how_it_helps.text: Establishes a competitive federal grant program requiring hospitals, starting within a year, to eliminate all eligible medical debt owed to them, prioritizing safety-net hospitals that agree to cancel recent debt owed by low-income patients from emergency and non-elective care, and expanding within two years to other providers and individuals.

Amends the Fair Debt Collection Practices Act to prohibit any debt collector or creditor from collecting medical debt incurred before enactment, with a private right of action letting consumers sue for compensatory and punitive damages plus attorney's fees.

Adds medical debt to the list of information excluded from consumer credit reports under the Fair Credit Reporting Act, effective 30 days after enactment, so unpaid medical bills can no longer drag down credit scores.

Requires providers to check whether a patient qualifies for charity care before payment is due, send a plain-language statement of what is owed within 30 days of a missed payment with language assistance in the 15 most common languages, bar interest on past-due medical payments, and cap what tax-exempt nonprofit hospitals can collect from uninsured patients.

analysis.who_pays: Taxpayers fund the grant program (the bill sets no dollar amount in its text); hospitals must comply with new billing, charity-care screening, and no-interest rules; medical debt collectors and credit bureaus lose revenue from collecting and reporting medical debt.
analysis.who_pays_short: Taxpayers, hospitals, debt collectors, credit bureaus

drawbacks.text: The grant program pays hospitals to erase debt that may have been unlikely to be collected in full anyway, and the bill sets no funding amount in its text, so the taxpayer cost of buying out hospitals' receivables is unaddressed.

Cancellation is a one-time fix that does not change the prices and billing practices that create medical debt; going forward, hospitals are only prioritized, not required, to cancel recent debt owed by low-income patients from emergency care.

The blanket ban on collecting any medical debt incurred before enactment, backed by a private right of action with punitive damages, sweeps in every provider and creditor holding such debt and would likely face legal challenges.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For people with medical debt, the benefits are large and immediate: bills erased, collections stopped, credit reports cleaned up, and interest stopped. The main honest costs are the taxpayer price of paying hospitals for their receivables, which the bill does not size, and the fact that it treats the symptom — one-time erasure — while only lightly regulating the billing and pricing practices that keep generating the debt.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced, referred to the Energy and Commerce and Financial Services Committees and then to a Health subcommittee, and never moved again before the two-year Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Ro Khanna introduced the Medical Debt Cancellation Act in the House on May 8, 2024, with 12 Democratic cosponsors.
The same day, it was referred to both the Energy and Commerce Committee and the Financial Services Committee; no committee scheduled a hearing or markup.
On May 17, 2024, it was referred to the Health Subcommittee, and the bill took no further action for the rest of the 118th Congress.
The Congress ended on January 3, 2025, and the bill died without ever receiving a floor vote in either chamber.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Medical debt collectors and credit bureaus keep the existing business of chasing and reporting unpaid medical bills, and hospitals avoid new billing and interest limits; the tens of millions of Americans holding medical debt are left exactly where they were.

sides.party_line_note: All 13 sponsors and cosponsors were House Democrats; no Republican signed on, and the bill never advanced in the Republican-controlled House.

industries.note: The bill makes it illegal to collect any pre-enactment medical debt and exposes collectors to consumer lawsuits with punitive damages. Their revenue depends on pursuing exactly the debt this bill cancels, so their gain runs against patients' relief.

industries.industry: Credit bureaus and consumer reporting agencies
industries.note: Medical debt would be barred from credit reports within 30 days, cutting off a data stream the bureaus include in scores they sell. Patients benefit directly from the same change.

Hospitals would be paid through federal grants to cancel patient debt they hold, and patients get the same relief — their interests run together here. The offsetting costs are new charity-care screening, plain-language billing, no interest on past-due balances, and collection caps for nonprofit hospitals.
